title: Quickfold SDK Handoff Cheatsheet (draft)
content:
Purpose:
A compact, action-oriented cheatsheet for shipping an SDK integration from internal handoff -> first-demo -> production smoke tests. This doc is designed for small cross-functional "cadet" workshops (30–60 minutes) where an engineer with limited time can onboard an internal integrator or partner, run a smoke demo, and leave with a reproducible checklist.

Audience:
- Solutions engineers, partner integrators, developer advocates, and new hire engineers who need a minimal but robust handoff path.

High-level goals for a 30–60 minute session:
1) Confirm environment and credentials (5–10m)
2) Run a zero-to-demo quickstart (10–20m)
3) Execute smoke tests and observe telemetry (10–15m)
4) Capture follow-ups and handoff artifacts (5–10m)

Preflight (what to prepare before the session):
- Repo and branch: point to a single demo branch (examples/quickfold-demo).
- Sandbox org: provision a short-lived sandbox API key with scoped permissions (tokens should expire in 30d).
- CI check: ensure ci/smoke.yml passes on branch.
- Minimal sample app: single-file example in Node or Python that runs end-to-end with 3 API calls (auth -> inference -> usage report).
- Telemetry sink: make sure the session audience has access to the demo trace dashboard for the model/route used.
- Short README: 1-page with 6 commands to get running.

Quick 6-command README (copyable):
1) git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/examples.git && cd examples/quickfold-demo
2) cp .env.example .env && edit API_KEY
3) npm install (or pip install -r requirements.txt)
4) npm run start-demo (or python demo.py)
5) open http://localhost:3000/demo and click "Run"
6) check telemetry dashboard: /console/traces?trace=quickfold-demo

Zero-to-demo script (narration for the handoff):
- Step 1 (1m): Quick orientation — show directory, demo file, and where to insert key.
- Step 2 (3m): Copy keys and run first command; show successful auth response.
- Step 3 (5m): Walk through the sample request payload and expected response. Point out model selection knob, temperature, and streaming flag.
- Step 4 (5m): Trigger the demo and read the output live. Note latency and token cost in the console.
- Step 5 (3m): Show console traces and per-request breakdown: tokens, latency, infra region.
- Step 6 (2m): Toggle a failure mode (invalid key or network) and show fallback behavior.

Minimal smoke test matrix (run after demo):
- Auth: invalid token -> 401 within 200ms. (expected)
- Simple generation: small prompt -> response starts streaming in < 400ms for local tests.
- Long prompt: 2x typical length -> KV cache behavior observed, latency increases but response completes.
- Rate limit: burst 30 req/s (in sandbox) -> observe 429 and retry header.
- Telemetry propagation: trace id present in response header and shows up on dashboard.

Telemetry & observability checks (what to watch):
- Verify per-request trace includes: route, model version, node id, kernel selection tag, and batch size.
- Confirm cost tokens emitted to cost service and visible on sample route dashboard.
- Error breakdown: look for model mismatch, OOM, or decoding errors.
- Alerting: demo should create no new alerts; if it does, capture the alertlink.

Key configuration knobs to highlight to integrators:
- modelRoute vs modelId: route is stable; id can change for rollouts. Recommend pinning to route for dev/demo and switching to explicit version for prod.
- streaming: when to enable for UX vs cost tradeoff.
- batchHints: set expected concurrents to help scheduling.
- cachePrefix: use a stable prefix for repeated prompts to benefit KV caching.

Failure modes and immediate mitigations (cheat-sheet style):
- 401 / invalid-key: confirm token scope & copy/paste; rotate via admin console.
- 429 rate-limits: exponential backoff (jitter), reduce batch size.
- 5xx / OOM: fall back to smaller model route or switch to non-quantized variant.
- Stale model output: check model version pinned in request and confirm route rollout status.

Handoff artifacts to capture at end of session:
- Demo branch + commit hash used.
- Sandbox token id and expiration.
- Links to: demo app, telemetry trace, failing replay (if any), and relevant Jira ticket.
- Short bullet list of next steps with owners and due dates (example below).

Example post-session follow-ups (template):
- Action: create persistent demo org for partner (Owner: Jonah, Due: +3d)
- Action: add integration test to CI (Owner: Marco, Due: +7d)
- Action: add model pin for production route (Owner: Integrator, Due: +14d)

CI smoke tests snippet (high-level):
- Test 1: smoke-auth -> call /v1/auth with sandbox token.
- Test 2: small-gen -> call example endpoint; assert response non-empty and latency < 2s.
- Test 3: trace-prop -> assert X-Trace-Id header returned.
- Implementation note: keep tests permissive for rate limits in sandbox (use retries).

Security and compliance checklist (quick):
- Do not commit API keys. Use .env and CI secrets.
- Use least privilege sandbox tokens.
- For customer demos containing PII: enable PII redaction plugin or use synthetic data.
- Ensure audit logs for demo org are enabled if partner requests.

Session artifacts (what to upload to the ticket):
- demo-screenshot.png (output + trace overlay)
- demo-log.txt (commands run + results)
- sandbox-token-id.txt (token id only — not the secret)
- short video (optional) 1–2 min recorded run

Templates (copy-paste into notes):
- "Demo run completed on {YYYY-MM-DD} using commit {sha}. No blocking issues; follow-ups: {list}."
- "Observed unexpected 429 at ~10s into burst test — likely sandbox throttle; owner assigned: Marco."

Open questions for follow-up (capture during session):
- Does partner need dedicated capacity or can they share a small reserved pool?
- What SLOs do they expect for 95th/99th percentile latency?
- Any data residency constraints?

Notes to self (tips learned from past workshops):
- Keep the sample app to a single file — fewer moving parts reduces friction.
- Use synthetic prompts that are representative of production but safe to share.
- Prewarm kernels by running one heavy request before demo to avoid a cold-start surprise.
- If network flakiness appears, switch to recorded response to continue the walkthrough.

Appendix: quick troubleshooting commands
- Validate token: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/auth/validate
- Run a simple gen: curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" -d '{"prompt":"hello"}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate
- Fetch last 20 traces: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_KEY" https://console.redwood.ai/api/traces?limit=20

Intended next steps for this doc:
- Move to a one-page printable handout (A4) for SE cadets.
- Add a short video and micro-lab exercises for self-serve learning.
- Convert CI snippets into a reusable GitHub Action.

If you run this session and something unexpected happens, add a one-line note to this doc describing the symptom and what you tried — we will incorporate real failure modes into the next revision.

-- end of cheatsheet draft --
